title: How Will We Train Developers If AI Does the Routine Work: A Conversation with Scott Hanselman
gist: Microsoft/GitHub VP Scott Hanselman argues AI generates features well but designs architecture poorly, and proposes borrowing nursing's 'preceptor' model -- dedicated trainers measured on how many engineers they mint, not code shipped -- to prevent the junior engineer pipeline from collapsing as AI absorbs the entry-level 'toil' work new engineers traditionally learned from; he also warns that remote work, social media, and AI are compounding to isolate developers and erode flow state.

themes.theme: AI is good at features, bad at architecture

insights.claim: Hanselman states that AI generates software features extremely well but does not generate architecture well, tending to be myopic and missing the big picture, citing a real current example where AI built a 'god object' super-struct into his application over several weeks that now needs to be removed before it collapses under its own weight.
insights.speaker: Scott Hanselman
insights.so_what: A concrete, named architectural failure mode (AI-introduced god objects) from a senior GitHub/Microsoft engineer using production AI coding tools daily — direct evidence that current AI coding agents need human architectural oversight, relevant to any team scaling agentic coding without senior review gates.
insights.quote: I have said recently on podcasts that AIs generate features extremely well. They do not generate architecture very well. They tend to be somewhat myopic in their view and they definitely miss the big picture.
insights.locator: AI is Not A Good Software Architect

insights.claim: Hanselman states plainly that human beings must keep their hands on the wheel and pushes back on the idea that AI will eventually write code for other AIs with no human review, framing continued human code review as something he will 'always fight for.'
insights.speaker: Scott Hanselman
insights.so_what: A senior industry insider explicitly rejecting the 'fully autonomous AI-to-AI coding' end state pushes back against more aggressive automation narratives — relevant for calibrating expectations of near-term full-autonomy coding-agent products.
insights.quote: Human beings have got to keep their hands on the wheel. That's the thing I will always fight for.

insights.claim: Hanselman describes his current daily workflow as reviewing diffs and pull requests from multiple engineers and AI, coordinating which of five pull requests from four different people to merge based on architectural soundness and whether 'slop' is creeping in, framing his role as a sculptor/teacher walking around making small corrective changes rather than a primary code author.
insights.speaker: Scott Hanselman
insights.so_what: Describes a concrete emerging senior-engineer role shape under AI-heavy workflows: reviewer/curator/architecture-gatekeeper rather than code author — a template for how senior IC roles may restructure as agentic coding scales.
insights.quote: I feel like a sculptor, but I'm really the teacher in a sculpting class and I'm walking around making small changes to everyone else's work.
insights.locator: Engineers and the Future Use of AI

themes.theme: The preceptor model for training junior engineers

insights.claim: Hanselman and Mark Russinovich argue in their Communications of the ACM piece that the software industry should adopt nursing's 'preceptor' model: a dedicated role whose explicit, formal job is training new engineers, with annual performance reviews based on whether they successfully mint new senior engineers rather than on code shipped.
insights.speaker: Scott Hanselman
insights.so_what: Proposes a concrete, exportable organizational structure (formalized preceptor role with training-outcome-based metrics) for any engineering org facing junior-pipeline collapse due to AI absorbing entry-level tasks — actionable for HR/eng-management tooling vendors and enterprise L&D budgets.
insights.quote: That trainer's job is not to ship code, but to ship engineers.
insights.locator: The Role of a Preceptor is to Create Engineers

insights.claim: Hanselman argues the core training problem is that junior engineers traditionally learned skills by doing the 'wax on, wax off' toil and tedium of routine work, and if AI now does that toil, there's a real open question about what altitude entry-level engineers should start at and whether skipping that foundational work is viable.
insights.speaker: Scott Hanselman
insights.so_what: Articulates the structural risk driving the entire preceptorship proposal: if AI removes the 'practice reps' junior engineers used to get, there is no established substitute skill-building path yet — a genuine talent-pipeline risk for the software industry over a 5-10 year horizon.
insights.quote: It is through the 'wax the car' that you learn karate. And if that job is now done by AI, then at what altitude... does an early in career person enter?
insights.locator: The Preceptor Model For Training Software Engineers

insights.claim: Microsoft has piloted the preceptor model with a group of about 400 people and completed its first cohort of preceptors, which Hanselman describes as successful; he says the approach is easier in small/midsize organizations (his personal comfort zone is 400-500 person companies) but is achievable in large companies like Microsoft when executed in shards with explicit executive buy-in and support.
insights.speaker: Scott Hanselman
insights.so_what: A concrete, named pilot (Microsoft, ~400 people, first cohort complete) gives investors and HR leaders an actual reference implementation and scale point to evaluate before adopting a similar training-role restructuring elsewhere.
insights.quote: We just finished our first cohort of preceptors and it's been very successful.

insights.claim: Hanselman frames preceptorship investment as costing money in the short term with payoff only after a couple of years, comparable to a fitness regimen, and warns that companies which fail to grow their own senior engineers will eventually be forced to poach them from competitors, absorbing that competitor's techniques and culture rather than their own.
insights.speaker: Scott Hanselman
insights.so_what: Frames underinvestment in junior-engineer training as a multi-year deferred cost that surfaces as forced, expensive competitive poaching later — a long-horizon labor-market risk model relevant to tech-sector HR cost forecasting and executive compensation incentive design (which tends to be quarterly, not multi-year).
insights.quote: The only way that they can get senior engineers is by poaching them from their competitor. And those senior engineers use their competitor's techniques and their competitor's culture.

insights.claim: Microsoft measures a metric called 'engineering thrive' or 'time to first PR,' explicitly framed not as a productivity metric but as a morale metric measuring how enabled and personally-growing a new hire feels when landing even a one-line pull request in their first days.
insights.speaker: Scott Hanselman
insights.so_what: A concrete, named internal metric ('time to first PR' as morale, not productivity) that other engineering organizations could adopt to measure onboarding health in an AI-heavy development environment.
insights.quote: It's not a productivity metric. It's not... a morale metric. Think about how exciting it will be for them to land their first PR.

themes.theme: Root cause: hyper-optimization, not AI itself

insights.claim: Hanselman argues the decline in entry-level hiring since 2017 (referenced in a Wall Street Journal study) is more attributable to general shortsighted hyper-optimization and late-stage capitalism's quarter-by-quarter planning horizon than to AI specifically, contending that businesses lack the same long-term perspective a senior engineer nearing retirement naturally develops.
insights.speaker: Scott Hanselman
insights.so_what: A named industry insider explicitly separates AI-driven job displacement fears from a broader, pre-existing corporate short-termism problem — implies policy/HR interventions should target quarterly-incentive structures, not just AI adoption itself, to fix the junior pipeline.
insights.quote: AI is not going to take your job. The hyper optimization of some C-suite executive is going to take your job.
insights.locator: AI Contributes to the Pre-existing Hyperoptimization of Business

insights.claim: Hanselman explicitly states that if AI makes him 20% more productive, the appropriate response would be reduced work hours (e.g., Fridays off) rather than proportionally higher output expectations, framing infinite compounding productivity growth applied to a finite human system as definitionally cancerous.
insights.speaker: Scott Hanselman
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to the prevailing corporate assumption that AI productivity gains should be captured entirely as more output rather than partially as reduced labor time — relevant to future labor-policy and compensation debates around AI productivity dividends.
insights.quote: This idea of constant, ongoing, forever emergent, infinite growth, that's cancer. So, if AI makes me 20% more productive, okay, 20%, maybe I get Fridays off. But that's not working.
insights.locator: Artificial Intelligence with a Humanistic Perspective

themes.theme: Remote work, social media, and AI-driven developer isolation

insights.claim: Hanselman argues remote work is not helping grow people, particularly early-career engineers, and describes a 'collapse of the third place' where work, home, and social life all happen in the same physical location, which he says prevents developers from becoming fully formed, healthy individuals.
insights.speaker: Scott Hanselman
insights.so_what: A senior Microsoft leader explicitly stating remote work is net-negative for junior developer growth is a notable data point for the ongoing return-to-office debate in tech, especially paired with a concrete organizational response (his own recurring in-person trips to Seattle every 4-6 weeks).
insights.quote: If work, home and the third place are all the same place. I don't know how you can grow into a fully formed and healthy individual.
insights.locator: The Collapse of the Third Place

insights.claim: Hanselman characterizes the current environment as 'the perfect storm of COVID, remote work, social media addiction and AI' threatening to harm young people's development, and cites recent Harvard Business Review-referenced research finding AI-powered engineers are getting more done but are lonelier, plus separate research finding people are losing access to flow state and that this is making them sad.
insights.speaker: Scott Hanselman
insights.so_what: Names a specific, citable research trend (AI use correlating with loneliness and loss of flow state) that investors in developer-tooling and workplace-wellness products should track as a growing counter-narrative to pure AI-productivity marketing.
insights.quote: It's the perfect storm of COVID, remote work, social media addiction and AI that threatens to break the young people.
insights.locator: The Collapse of the Third Place

insights.claim: Hanselman predicts that as AI moves into more embodied forms (robots walking around the house, a Roomba talking back and second-guessing instructions), anthropomorphization-driven problematic human behavior will increase, referencing the film Her as a non-aspirational cautionary example rather than a goal.
insights.speaker: Scott Hanselman
insights.so_what: A forward-looking risk flag on embodied/voice AI products (robots, smart home devices) becoming more emotionally entangling as they gain physical presence — relevant to product design and mental-health risk assessment for AI hardware companies.
insights.quote: I think when AI turns into a robot and starts walking around the house or when the Roomba starts talking back to you, you're going to see even more problematic behaviors.
insights.locator: The Danger For Engineers of Anthromorphizing AI

themes.theme: Agile and SDLC in the agentic era

insights.claim: Hanselman argues AI has not killed agile but has taken it to a ridiculous conclusion — 'too agile' — where combining agile's already-fast inner/outer loops with AI-driven speed causes the process to 'wobble at speed' like a car with wheels spinning too fast, potentially flying off the road.
insights.speaker: Scott Hanselman
insights.so_what: A vivid, quotable framework ('too agile') for diagnosing process breakdown in AI-accelerated software teams — useful mental model for engineering leaders evaluating whether their AI-accelerated delivery cadence has outrun their governance/review capacity.
insights.quote: When you combine agile... and then you apply AI to it, you get wheels that spin so fast that they kind of wobble at speed and then the car potentially flies off the road.

insights.claim: Hanselman states that new computer science/software engineering graduates cannot understand the full SDLC (software development lifecycle) from coursework alone, since college projects like 'connect four' are typically completed solo or in groups of three or four people, arguing this reinforces the need for senior-year internships and cohorts spent substantially in industry.
insights.speaker: Scott Hanselman
insights.so_what: Direct critique of university CS/software engineering curricula's inability to teach real-world SDLC — supports increased industry investment in structured internship/cohort programs as a complement to (or partial substitute for) academic training.
insights.locator: Preceptorship and Teaching Software in College

insights.claim: Hanselman warns that if the industry does not solve the junior/early-career engineer pipeline problem now, companies will eventually need to bring retired senior engineers back out of retirement to fix critical systems, drawing a direct parallel to Y2K remediation, and jokes he expects to be pulled out of retirement in 2035 for 'the next big date bug.'
insights.speaker: Scott Hanselman
insights.so_what: A specific, dated prediction (2035, next major date-bug-style crisis) tied to pipeline collapse — a long-horizon systemic risk for any organization dependent on legacy systems maintained by an aging, non-replenished senior engineer population.
insights.quote: We'll be bringing old people back out of retirement, just like Y2K. And they're going to go and pull me out of retirement in 2035 to go and fix the next big date bug.
insights.locator: Preceptorship and Teaching Software in College

insights.claim: Hanselman notes that 'architect' (like 'CTO') is a largely self-appointed, informally defined title in software with no standardized credentialing path, contrasting his own software engineering degree (the practice of shipping) against computer science degrees (compiler theory, computational theory), and argues the ideal preparation would combine both.
insights.speaker: Scott Hanselman
insights.so_what: Useful framing for hiring/HR teams: 'architect' titles carry no standardized skill guarantee industry-wide, so credential-based hiring filters for that title may be unreliable signals of actual capability.
insights.quote: Architect is one of those titles that one could probably just give themselves like CTO.
insights.locator: How Did You Become An Architect?
